reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Six-second contact sampling over full reference, burned-in English and exact phase/frame labels read; no all-frame or full-audio-listening claim.
reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.

centralQuestion: How can the moment after a button press feel immediate while still conveying the force of an upcoming attack?
thesis: Make input acceptance visually apparent immediately, then choose the lead-in's duration and shape for the specific attack; responsiveness does not mean removing every windup.
titleCorrection: Do not reduce this lesson to why anticipation is always necessary; it explicitly shows attacks with practically no lead-in.

claims: Lead-in is the pose interval after the button press and before the actual attack, also called anticipation or windup.
sections.observedVisuals: Pit attack on the grid and a reference to the preceding phase lesson.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Reuse our A03 mannequin and timeline, enlarge only the input-to-attack interval.
prerequisites: Separate input recognition from attack collision becoming active.
sections.transitionToNext: A charged attack holds this part of the pose, making it easy to examine.

claims: Smash Ultimate charge poses hold and tremble during the lead-in.
sections.observedVisuals: Several grid-isolated fighters including Wario and Luigi hold a charged smash pose.
sections.exampleRoles: Expose the preparation pose without needing to infer it from a very fast complete strike.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Our character presses, enters a windup and holds it on the grid; show charge as a distinct state, not the universal behavior of every attack.
sections.transitionToNext: The pose is readable because its change starts as soon as the input is accepted.

claims: Large changes can occur on the first animation frame to prioritize responsiveness.
A more gradual interpolation from idle would be smoother but could hide input feedback.
External network/display delay may exist, but the game's accepted input should receive prompt visible reaction.
sections.observedVisuals: Link and Pyra frame-zero/frame-one split comparisons; further big-change examples with Sheik, Isabelle and Wii Fit Trainer.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Same-camera same-character A/B with input dot and first pose change marker; one version spends several frames near idle, the other reaches a readable preparation pose immediately. Our timings must be labeled illustrative.
prerequisites: Define interpolation as filling the poses between two specified poses; show it before naming it.
Distinguish game reaction timing from unmeasured network/display latency.
sections.transitionToNext: An attack can even begin with almost no preparation, but that is a design choice rather than a universal target.

claims: Some attacks have effectively no lead-in.
The source identifies Zero Suit Samus's neutral attack as appearing one frame after the reaction.
Final Fight's rapidly repeated jab shows the appeal of immediate response.
sections.observedVisuals: Zero Suit Samus labeled frame-one jab on grid, then Final Fight Cody jab footage.
sections.exampleRoles: A precise edge case disproves the idea that every attack must have a visible long windup; another game confirms responsive repetition.
sections.ownScreenProposal: If the exact game/frame claim is retained, obtain separate eligible footage and corroborate timing. Otherwise show our zero/short-windup attack as an explicit illustration beside independent responsive gameplay.
sections.transitionToNext: Eliminating preparation also removes functions that some games or attacks need.

claims: In some online games, the windup period can help cover network-related delay.
A strong preparation shape can contribute to the visual feeling of a heavy attack.
Making every attack as fast as possible is not always the best design.
sections.observedVisuals: King Dedede and Bowser substantial attack movements on grid.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Keep total intent clear: compare a light jab and a heavier windup without claiming measured latency. A simple conceptual network timeline can illustrate possible coverage, labeled as illustration rather than a specific game's netcode.
sections.transitionToNext: Judge the lead-in by what the player can see immediately and what the attack must communicate.

claims: Consider lead-in design from the standpoint of clearly communicating input acceptance.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Replay input dot → immediate readable windup → strike on our same grid, retaining the distinction between recognition and impact.
sections.transitionToNext: End at the concrete responsive result; no unrelated netcode lesson.

canonicalTerms.note: Do not imply every use of lead-in, startup and external input latency is interchangeable.

omissionsAndReasons: Omit prior-video promotional wording; supply the needed phase definition here.
Retain the no-lead-in counterexample and the speed-versus-weight balance; they are necessary explanation, not redundant hedges.
